title: The Table of Nations
summary: The chapter lists the descendants of Noah's three sons, Japheth, Ham, and Shem, and the peoples and territories that came from them after the flood. It pauses to describe Nimrod, a mighty hunter who founded kingdoms in Babylonia and Assyria, and to trace the borders of Canaan and the line of Shem through Eber. It ends by saying that from these clans the nations spread out over the earth.
story: God told Noah's family to fill the earth (9:1, 7), and this chapter shows them doing it. It is a map of the known world drawn as a family tree, and it sets the stage for the rest of Genesis. Chapter 11 will tell how the peoples were scattered at Babel, and then the story will narrow to one man, Abram, a descendant of Shem through Eber. Before God chooses one family, the Bible pauses to name the whole world. Israel does not even appear in the list. That is deliberate: the nations come first, and when God calls Abram, it will be so that all the families of the earth may be blessed through him.
historical:
Many of the names can be connected with peoples known from ancient records, though some remain uncertain. Among Japheth's sons, Madai is the Medes of Iran, Javan the Ionian Greeks, Gomer probably the Cimmerians known from Assyrian texts, and Tubal and Meshech peoples of Anatolia (modern Turkey). Kittim points to Cyprus, and Tarshish to a distant western port, often placed in Spain. Among Ham's sons, Cush is the land south of Egypt (ancient Nubia), Mizraim is the ordinary Hebrew name for Egypt, and Put is probably Libya; several descendants of Cush (Sheba, Dedan, Havilah) were peoples of Arabia, linked to Africa by trade across the Red Sea. Among Shem's sons, Elam lay in southwestern Iran, Asshur is Assyria, and Aram the Arameans of Syria.

Nimrod's kingdom names the great cities of Mesopotamia: Babylon, Erech (Uruk), and Accad in the south, and in the north Nineveh and Calah, the Assyrian capitals. Scholars have proposed several historical kings or legendary figures behind Nimrod, but none has been confirmed. The Philistines are said to come from the Casluhites; elsewhere the Bible says they came from Caphtor, usually identified with Crete (Amos 9:7), and some think the parenthesis originally stood after the Caphtorites. The Hittites listed among Canaan's sons were residents of Canaan, and their relation to the Hittite empire of Anatolia is debated.
cultural:
Ancient peoples often expressed their relationships to one another in the language of family: nations were sons, cities were daughters, and alliances were brotherhoods. The table uses that language, but its categories are broader than biology. Each section closes by naming clans, languages, lands, and nations (verses 5, 20, and 31), and the grouping reflects geography, political ties, and history as much as descent. The Canaanites spoke a language closely related to Hebrew but are listed under Ham, while the Elamites spoke a language unrelated to Hebrew and are listed under Shem. The chapter is not a modern ethnic or linguistic classification, and it was never meant to rank peoples.

For an Israelite reader the list was full of meaning. It named Israel's great enemies (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon), its neighbors (the Canaanite peoples, Aram), and the distant peoples of the coastlands and islands. Every one of them was placed in the same family as Israel, descended from Noah. The borders of Canaan in verse 19, from Sidon in the north to Gaza in the south and east toward Sodom, sketch the land that God will promise to Abraham.
literary: The table follows the heading of 10:1 (This is the account of Noah's sons) and deals with the sons in reverse order of importance: Japheth first, then Ham, then Shem, whose line the story will follow. Genesis regularly treats the side branches first and the main line last. The list is mostly spare, with a repeated formula (the sons of X), but it breaks off twice for short narratives. The first is about Nimrod, the first person called a mighty one after the flood, a builder of cities and kingdoms whose name became proverbial. The second is a brief note about Peleg, whose name means division, because in his days the earth was divided. Traditional counting yields about seventy names, and later Jewish tradition spoke of seventy nations of the world, the same number as the members of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (46:27). Chapter 11 then tells the story that explains how these divisions of language came about, so the two chapters are arranged by theme rather than strict chronology.

outline.t: The descendants of Japheth: the peoples of the coastlands
The descendants of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan
Nimrod and the kingdoms of Babylonia and Assyria
Egypt's descendants and the clans and borders of Canaan
The descendants of Shem through Eber and Joktan
The nations spread out over the earth

doctrines.note: Every nation in the known world is traced back to one family, and through Noah to Adam. The chapter teaches the unity of the human race beneath its many languages and territories. No people stands outside the human family or outside God's concern.

The spread of the nations fulfills God's command to fill the earth. The borders and territories named here are not random; Scripture later says that God determined the boundaries of the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8; Acts 17:26). History unfolds under his hand, even among peoples who do not know him.

The chapter names the nations before God calls Abram, and it does not mention Israel at all. God's plan to bless all the families of the earth through Abraham (12:3) begins with a world already named and known to him. The table is the backdrop for the whole biblical story of God's purpose for the nations.

words.note: Goy, nation. In the Old Testament it can be used of Israel, but it came to be used mostly of the other peoples, the nations or Gentiles. It appears here in the refrain of verses 5, 20, 31, and 32. God will promise Abraham that he will become a great goy (12:2), taking his place among the nations listed here in order to bless them.

Mishpachah, clan or family, a group larger than a household and smaller than a tribe or nation. It is the word used in 12:3 when God promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram. The families named in this chapter are the ones that promise has in view.

Gibbor, mighty man, warrior, or hero. It was used in 6:4 for the mighty men of old before the flood. Nimrod is the first to become one after it, a hunter and builder of kingdoms. The word itself is neutral and is later used of David's warriors, but here it hints at the return of the pride and power that marked the world before the flood.

Palag, to divide, the verb behind the name Peleg in verse 25. A related noun means a water channel (as in Psalm 1:3). Most interpreters take the division as the scattering of peoples at Babel in chapter 11; some suggest a division of land by irrigation canals or of Eber's family into two branches. The text gives no more detail.

christ: The New Testament picks up the world of this chapter and shows God's purpose for it. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God “made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands” (Acts 17:26), echoing the table's picture of one human family spread across the earth. Jesus sent his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and the Bible's closing vision shows “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). The nations that separated here are gathered there. Some scholars also connect the seventy (or, in some manuscripts, seventy-two) disciples Jesus sends out in Luke 10:1 with the nations of this chapter, a suggestive but uncertain link. The chapter itself does not predict Christ. It names the world that God has not given up on, the world the promise to Abraham and its fulfillment in Christ are meant to reach.
questions: Israel's greatest enemies, Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon, appear in this list as members of the same human family. How does that challenge the way you think about people you see as rivals or enemies?
God names the nations before he calls Abraham. What does that suggest about his concern for peoples and places far from your own?
Nimrod is remembered as a mighty man and a builder of kingdoms. What kinds of power and achievement does our culture admire, and how does Genesis invite us to see them?
